gist: Freelancer.com CEO Matt Barrie gives Erik Townsend a hands-on account of running ~40 personal AI agents that burned 4 billion tokens in a single day at $1,300, then walks the cost stack down 500x by switching to Chinese open models and buying his own Nvidia DGX Spark boxes — arguing the open models win the token market, Nvidia is deliberately going direct-to-user around a $1.65 trillion debt-financed data-center buildout whose demand rests on two customers, and white-collar queue jobs are about to be automated wholesale. The back half is MacroVoices' usual market segment: a long-dated Nvidia call trade, oil breaking $100, collapsing S&P breadth, and extreme grain positioning.

themes.theme: Agentic AI inside a live operating company

insights.claim: Freelancer.com's CEO personally built a fleet of about 40-44 agents in roughly a month, automating team workflows such as project-approval queue processing that previously required about 11 people to staff 24/7.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Queue-shaped headcount is the first cost line to fall in any services business; screen portfolio companies and labor-intensive listed businesses for the share of staff sitting in repetitive queues.
insights.quote: in the space of about two sessions of half an hour to an hour you can now completely automate that queue processing

insights.claim: After a performance marketer resigned, the role was replaced by an agent that reads Google Ads, Google Analytics, the database, financial performance, shipped code and the ticketing system overnight and delivers a tuning report at 4:10am — against a roughly half-million-dollar monthly ad spend.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: The economics are decisive when the agent manages a large spend line: a 10% improvement on $500k/month of ad spend dwarfs the token bill, which is the template for where agents get deployed first.
insights.quote: no human, no matter how much I looked into the market to find someone great. There's no way that they'll be getting up every morning at 4:00 a.m. and producing a report by 4:10

insights.claim: The agent fleet consumed 4 billion tokens in a single day at a cost of roughly $1,300, of which about $900 was Anthropic's Sonnet-tier model — and roughly 3 billion of those 4 billion tokens were prompt-cache reads generated by agents looping on polling schedules.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Prompt caching means headline token counts massively overstate real inference demand; anyone modelling token-growth-to-revenue for model providers needs to net out cache reads.
insights.quote: it came in at um 4 billion tokens in one day and that's 4 billion with a B

insights.claim: A single prompt instructing the agent system to optimize itself for cost cut token usage by a further 85%, on top of the savings already available from model switching.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Agent inference spend is highly elastic and self-optimizing, which argues against extrapolating current per-customer token revenue for the labs.
insights.quote: by just typing in that one single prompt I managed to optimize the token usage down by another 85%

insights.claim: AI now handles 100% of Freelancer.com's tier-one customer interactions, delivering instant 24/7 responses in any language with answers described as four times longer, four times better and ten times more empathetic than human agents could sustain.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-shipped datapoint for the BPO and contact-centre disruption thesis rather than a projection.
insights.quote: AI now does 100% of our tier one uh interactions with customers

insights.claim: The agentic stack is no longer gated on specialist talent — a building maintenance handyman with no coding background taught himself to script APIs and build his own dashboards with Claude Code as a hobby.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend, host
insights.so_what: If adoption does not require expensive consultants, the diffusion curve is far steeper than enterprise-software analogues imply — bullish for token demand, bearish for implementation-services businesses.
insights.quote: That says to me that this whole thing can happen way faster with far less specialized human skill than I ever imagined.

themes.theme: Inference cost curve and model arbitrage

insights.claim: The same day's agent workload costs roughly $80,000 on an Opus-class model, $1,300 the way it was actually run, and about $150 on the Chinese open model GLM 5.3 — a 500x spread available purely by switching models.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: A 500x price dispersion for near-equivalent output is the single strongest argument that frontier-model pricing is not defensible; it caps the revenue case underwriting the data-center buildout.
insights.quote: that's $80,000 in Opus, $1,300 the way I did it, $150 on GM 5.3, which is a 500x spread, just switch between models

insights.claim: There are effectively zero switching costs between models — a slash-command in a coding harness reloads the context into a different model, and an agent can be migrated between harnesses by asking it to write its own transfer file.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: No customer lock-in means model providers have no pricing power at the commodity tier; the durable margin has to sit in hardware, distribution or verticals rather than the model itself.
insights.quote: There's zero switching costs. The agents have no loyalty.

insights.claim: Every conventional moat is absent in foundation models: the science sits in roughly 40 public technical papers, weights are open, and new state-of-the-art labs keep appearing from nowhere — DeepSeek, then Z.ai — making it the most brutally competitive market in the world.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Treat model-layer businesses as commodity producers, not software franchises, when underwriting their valuations.
insights.quote: the AI foundational models are like opening a Thai restaurant in a row full of other Thai restaurants in Thailand on steroids

insights.claim: Free frontier access is a training-data acquisition channel: when GLM 5.3 launched as 'Ox Alpha' it gave away 100 trillion tokens free, the model visibly improved over that week, and roughly 42 trillion tokens of user data went in as training material.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Free or heavily discounted inference should be read as a data trade, which is the core reason enterprises will eventually pay a premium for private inference.
insights.quote: if you're kind of wondering why, you know, why it's free, it's because you're probably the product

insights.claim: Current token prices are a teaser rate: the subsidised pricing is expected to reset upward once lenders financing the data-center buildout start repricing the underlying debt.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, with Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Businesses building agent workloads on current token prices are running an unhedged input-cost exposure; owning hardware is the hedge.
insights.quote: We're on still on the teaser rate for token pricing.

insights.claim: Anthropic's refusals are a commercial liability — the model declining to review the user's own legal documents on policy grounds is described as materially hurting adoption, while the open-source community removes refusals from every released open model within days through 'obliteration' fine-tunes.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Two implications: safety guardrails carry a measurable adoption cost for closed labs, and model-level safety policy is unenforceable once weights are public.
insights.quote: all this AI safety stuff that's going on, it's all pretty pointless with open source because every model out there has been obliterated

insights.claim: Astra is not delivering on its AGI marketing in practice — it failed six straight attempts to draw a border on a graphic, and users report it rewriting entire authentication systems when asked for a small change — while excelling narrowly at things like Blender 3D modelling.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Frontier launch cycles are accompanied by paid-influencer hype; the 'is everyone switching back to OpenAI' question is, on hands-on evidence, no.
insights.quote: I don't think Astra is kind of there yet

insights.claim: Anthropic may restrict access to its high-end API because Chinese labs buy subscriptions and distil the knowledge out of the models, pushing the market toward stratification: commodity tokens from Chinese open models, and the Western labs moving upmarket toward consulting-style engagements for pharma or defence.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: If the labs migrate into consulting-shaped revenue, they compete with McKinsey and Deloitte rather than with software vendors — a direct threat to high-end consulting margins.
insights.quote: you'd hate to be a Mckenzie or a deoid at this point in time

themes.theme: Local inference and the hardware scramble

insights.claim: A pair of Nvidia DGX Spark boxes (~$4,000 each at purchase, now around $5,000) with a 200GB memory link can run a 300-billion-parameter DeepSeek V4 Flash model at 45-60 tokens per second, described as Opus-level quality, at about $9,000 of hardware to power one programmer.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: A concrete price point at which local inference substitutes for a frontier subscription — the threshold that determines how much of the token market ever reaches the hyperscalers.
insights.quote: effectively a pair of DGXs can run DeepSc V4. You get kind of Opus level quality

insights.claim: Replicating the full 4-billion-token-per-day agent workload locally would take about 16 DGX Sparks at roughly $65,000 of hardware — about $100 a day amortised over two years plus roughly $8 a day of electricity, since each box draws only about 100 watts.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Owned hardware at ~$108/day versus $1,300/day of rented frontier tokens is the arbitrage that pulls inference to the edge and caps hyperscaler pricing.
insights.quote: It draws collectively less power than a kettle uh to boil because they're about 100 watts each.

insights.claim: The scramble for self-hosted inference hardware is already visible in supply: DGX Spark prices rose between two purchases, distributors went out of stock in the US and globally, and the Mikrotik switch that chains four boxes into 512GB of unified memory sold out worldwide.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Consumer and prosumer AI hardware shortages are a real-time demand signal for Nvidia's direct channel and for the memory chain feeding it.
insights.quote: by the time I hit reload on the page, they're out of stock

insights.claim: A secondary market in used data-center GPUs is booming as Hopper-series kit comes off lease ahead of Blackwell and Vera Rubin — it is about to become the second-largest category on escrow.com.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com and escrow.com
insights.so_what: A rare non-public window into GPU resale volumes; a liquid secondhand market puts a floor under residual values but also undercuts new-build leasing economics for the SPVs.

insights.claim: Enterprise is heading for an 'emperor has no clothes' moment on data privacy — everything in G Suite, on the public web and in hyperscaler-hosted email is being scraped and trained on, and traffic from AI scrapers to freelancer.com is up 1,300% in twelve months.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Names an explicit trillion-dollar opportunity in confidential/private AI, and flags a real cost line for content sites: CDN bills rising while blocking scrapers risks damaging search-driven customer acquisition.
insights.quote: I do think there's a trillion dollar industry available right now around confidentiality and privacy

insights.claim: Hugging Face has become the distribution hub where open models are quantized, obliterated and hardware-tuned by enthusiasts, which is framed as the reason Nvidia acquired it.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Reads Nvidia's move as buying the open-model distribution layer to pair with direct hardware sales — the vertical play that hedges its data-center customer concentration.

themes.theme: AI capex debt bomb and Nvidia going direct

insights.claim: Hyperscalers have loaded on roughly $1.65 trillion of debt over five years — about $500 billion from data centers and $200 billion from private credit — before counting off-balance-sheet vehicles, versus subprime peaking at $1.3 trillion in 2007 with 55 million mortgages behind it, while the AI buildout is underwritten by effectively two customers.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, citing Ed Zitron
insights.so_what: The central bear case on AI credit: the collateral pool has almost no diversification, so a stumble at either OpenAI or Anthropic transmits straight into data-center SPV debt and private credit marks.
insights.quote: Subprime peaked at 1.3 trillion in 2007. And that that was had 55 million mortgages behind it. While this AI explosion has two customers, OpenAI Anthropic.

insights.claim: Data-center special-purpose vehicles are structured to hold the chips, the debt and the risk off the sponsor's balance sheet — Meta is cited as carrying $46 billion of exposure to Hyperion in its filings with none of it on the balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, citing Ed Zitron
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet leverage screens understate hyperscaler AI exposure; read the filings' off-balance-sheet commitments before sizing credit risk.
insights.quote: data center special purpose vehicles are this bubble cos clarized debt obligations and AI data centers are at subprime mortgages

insights.claim: Customer concentration in cloud AI revenue is extreme: OpenAI and Anthropic are cited as accounting for roughly 73% of Amazon's AI revenue, 74% of Microsoft's, and over half of all Google Cloud by 2027.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler AI revenue growth is not a diversified secular trend but a two-counterparty story; stress-test cloud segment forecasts against those two names' funding.

insights.claim: Nvidia is deliberately sidestepping the coming data-center credit problem by selling boxes directly to end users, prosumers and enterprises — DGX Spark at roughly $5,000, a ~$100,000 station with about 748GB of memory — and letting the SPVs fight over the leases.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: The core bull case for Nvidia decoupling from an OpenAI blow-up: direct hardware revenue survives even if the rental/leasing complex breaks.
insights.quote: Nvidia is still out there in the market selling direct

insights.claim: Four of Nvidia's largest customers are now building their own chips, including an OpenAI inference chip described as roughly twice as efficient in watts per inference, which is part of why Nvidia is opening a direct channel.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Customer-designed inference silicon compresses Nvidia's future data-center share, making the direct/edge channel strategically necessary rather than opportunistic.

insights.claim: Nvidia resembles a software company in its cost structure — it packages high-bandwidth memory sourced from only three suppliers (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung) around a GPU at roughly 70% margin — leaving it dependent on that memory chain.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: HBM suppliers are the chokepoint with pricing leverage over Nvidia's margin; a reason to look at the memory names as a levered expression of the same demand.

insights.claim: Open models will win the bulk of the token market, which is the strategic premise behind Nvidia's direct-hardware and Hugging Face moves, even though the Western labs retain an agentic-reliability edge for now.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: If token volume migrates to open weights running on owned hardware, the revenue never reaches the hyperscalers that are financing the buildout — the crux of the AI capex bear case.
insights.quote: I think the open models are going to win here

insights.claim: On the amortised economics of owning data-center-class hardware: secondhand eight-GPU H100 boxes run $150,000-$200,000 for 5,000-10,000 tokens per second, while Blackwell B200 boxes at roughly $500,000 deliver 20,000-40,000 tokens per second — about $400-600/day and $700-900/day respectively.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Gives a defensible per-token cost floor for owned compute against which rented frontier token prices can be benchmarked.

themes.theme: White-collar dislocation and the skills that survive

insights.claim: The unit of organisational change is the functional team collapsing to a team leader plus AI — where a leader previously managed five people processing a queue, the AI becomes the team and the leader directs it.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: A specific model for headcount reduction that preserves management layers while eliminating individual contributors — the shape to look for in company disclosures.
insights.quote: It would be the team leader controlling the AI and the AI will be the team effectively.

insights.claim: Barrie would not want to be long commercial real estate — not because of work-from-home, but because AI is about to remove a large fraction of the white-collar jobs that occupy the buildings; an Australian bank with 50,000 employees and 700 branches could plausibly run on 10,000 or fewer.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: An explicit short/avoid on office CRE tied to a headcount mechanism rather than to hybrid work, and a template for screening bank cost bases.
insights.quote: I wouldn't be want to be long commercial real estate at the moment. It's not because the work from home. It's because it's the AI is going to chew through a lot of these jobs.

insights.claim: The scarce human skill in an agentic world is agency and initiative rather than technical specialisation, because the ability to execute an idea has collapsed to writing English in a chat harness.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: A hiring and career filter: the survivors of automation are the people who generate and direct work, which also argues for an explosion in one-person businesses.
insights.quote: So the most important thing you need to develop is as a human is agency.

insights.claim: The endpoint of white-collar automation is a hyper-competitive entrepreneurial society resembling India's informal economy — everyone running hustles and micro-businesses — following the historical pattern of agricultural and factory mechanisation.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: If correct, demand shifts toward tools, marketplaces and payment rails serving micro-entrepreneurs rather than toward enterprise seat-based software.

insights.claim: University value is now degree-specific: engineering-style degrees still teach analytic method and MBAs still sell a network, but most curricula teach material from ten to twenty years ago and will have to move to oral exams as AI breaks take-home assessment.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, former adjunct professor
insights.so_what: Structural pressure on the higher-education business model, with continuing/professional education the segment most likely to hold value.

insights.claim: Energy is the binding constraint on the singularity: if every person on earth burned 4 billion tokens a day it would require roughly 30 terawatts — many multiples of current world energy production — against planned data-center additions of only 200-300 gigawatts.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Quantifies why 'age of abundance' framings fail and why power generation, not chips, becomes the binding bottleneck and the durable investment theme.
insights.quote: energy is kind of the final boss that had need to be solved I think for the singularity to occur

insights.claim: The meaningful singularity milestone is AI improving AI without human participation, at which point outcomes are determined purely by who commits the most energy and GPUs — and research published this week on how much frontier-model code is now written by other AI suggests the process has begun.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend, host, with Matt Barrie
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable marker for AGI progress — the share of model code written by AI — that is more useful than benchmark or marketing claims.
insights.quote: The equation blows up when it can accelerate itself without human participation.

insights.claim: Jensen Huang has proclaimed AGI has arrived with Astra and Elon Musk publicly assigns an 80% base case of an abundance outcome alongside a 10-20% probability of human extinction — a range wide enough that the host treats it as unactionable framing.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend, host
insights.so_what: Executive AGI proclamations are marketing inputs into the capex cycle; treat them as sentiment indicators rather than forecasts.
insights.quote: there's also unfortunately an outlier case of 10, maybe even 20% probability of outcome, which is that it's an extinction event for the human race

insights.claim: Humanoid robotics has solved locomotion and is entering commercial scale — Unitree has IPO'd, is described as profitable with billions in revenue, and units start at around $6,000 with superhuman running and jumping performance.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Names the specific listed vehicle and the price point at which humanoid robots become deployable — the next capex wave venture capital is financing after AI models.
insights.quote: these things are selling starting at $6,000

themes.theme: Freelancer's positioning: humans as inference engines

insights.claim: Freelancer.com positions its 90 million-person marketplace as 'artificial artificial intelligence' — humans framed as 20-watt inference engines with free pre-training who already have access to every model — to sell AI automation projects into companies lacking in-house expertise.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: The labor marketplace is repositioning as the implementation channel for agentic AI rather than as roadkill — the key question for anyone valuing gig marketplaces in an AI world.
insights.quote: these humans are effectively 20 watt inference engines with free pre-training

insights.claim: The commercial weakness of raw AI is its nondeterminism — described as pay-to-pray, a slot machine where you sometimes go in circles — which is why paying per outcome rather than per token is pitched as the superior procurement model.
insights.speaker: Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com
insights.so_what: Outcome-based rather than token-based pricing is where service providers can defend margin against model commoditisation.
insights.quote: it's pay to prey. It's a slot machine.

themes.theme: Where's the trade: rates, oil and positioning

insights.claim: The recommended expression of the AI structural thesis is long-dated Nvidia optionality rather than the shares: with the stock around $224.31, a January 2027 at-the-money call trading near $21.60 at roughly 38% implied volatility and 128 days to expiration, because January 2027 implied vols have collapsed to the lowest levels of the past year.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: Defined-risk, positive-vega exposure that survives a correction into the midterms while retaining upside if semis re-accelerate — the cheap-vol argument is the actual edge here, not the direction.
insights.quote: January 2027 option implied volatilities have collapsed towards the lowest levels in the past year

insights.claim: The current market regime runs oil as the catalyst, the bond market as the transmission mechanism and equities as the absorber of the damage, with WTI printing $100 and Brent clearing it, forcing the front end to reprice toward more hawkish central bank action across the US, Canada and Europe.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: A clean causal chain for positioning: trade the oil shock through rates and equity multiples rather than only through energy equities.
insights.quote: oil has just been the catalyst and the bond market now is the transmission mechanism and now equities are absorbing all of this damage

insights.claim: The 10-year sits at 485 basis points and the 30-year back above 530, driven by heavy Treasury supply, fiscal concerns, rising term premium and enormous corporate borrowing competing for capital — and a $6 billion buyback announcement disappointed a market expecting $10 billion.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: A rising risk-free hurdle rate compresses equity valuations even without credit spreads widening — watch whether the stress stays confined to Treasuries.
insights.quote: that risk-free hurdle rate is rising, pressuring these equity valuations

insights.claim: Market breadth has collapsed from roughly 70% of S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day moving average a month ago to near 35%, with breakdowns across consumer discretionary, staples, retailers, industrials, defence, homebuilders, utilities, transports and REITs — masked at the index level by a pop in the mega-cap and semiconductor complex.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: Index level is hiding a broad internal breakdown; if semis lose their 50-day averages there is nothing left holding the index up.
insights.quote: I'd like to you think of it like a analogy of castle built on sand and the sand is shifting under the castle but the castle hasn't yet moved

insights.claim: CTA sell triggers cluster around 7,500-7,550 on the S&P — roughly 50 to 100 points below current levels — and crossing them could pivot $100 billion-plus of systematic flows, with the Russell having already rolled over.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host, citing Charlie McElligott and other quant desks
insights.so_what: A specific, monitorable level where mechanical selling begins — the most actionable risk marker in the episode.

insights.claim: The oil move is a physical supply story with a short squeeze on top: global inventories have fallen roughly 400 million barrels per EIA estimates, gross WTI short positioning hit a five-year extreme near 242,000 contracts in July, and large speculators still have not rebuilt length even as price rips.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: Unrebuilt speculative length into a genuine inventory drawdown means the squeeze may have further fuel; the test is whether WTI sustains above $100.
insights.quote: The global inventory buffer is dangerously thin.

insights.claim: Gold's two-year bull market ended with a January 2026 blowoff near 5,600 followed by a 25% bullion correction, but with speculative length rebuilt without becoming crowded and a weakening dollar offsetting rising real rates, the correction is judged close to over and dips should be bought.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: A buy-the-dip stance with an explicit caveat that consolidation could run a few more months into the midterms.

insights.claim: Uranium is near $90 on U3O8 with general accumulation, and uranium miners have broken out while correlating closely with gold miners — suggesting a combined precious-and-uranium equity basket.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: An underdiscussed correlation trade; if it persists, the two miner groups can be sized as one risk bucket rather than two.

insights.claim: The yen has broken above its 50-week moving average for the first time in roughly a year and a half of decisive downtrend, with large speculators still deeply net short after intervention — a setup for a larger carry-trade unwind if dips keep getting bought.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: A key breakout plus stale short positioning plus a weakening dollar is the classic configuration for a sustained trend change — high on the watch list into year-end.

insights.claim: Agricultural positioning is at a one-year and three-year 100th percentile across corn, wheat, soybeans, sugar, bean oil and bean meal, with corn's five-year-extreme gross shorts squeezed out over two months and gross and net longs now at five-year highs — crowded, but with genuine supply fundamentals behind it.
insights.speaker: Patrick, MacroVoices co-host
insights.so_what: Explicitly not a contrarian short yet — the lesson is that crowding alone is not a fade signal when supply risk is real, but it raises the fragility of grain longs.
insights.quote: crowding is not a contrarian trade right off the bat because there is genuine fundamentals behind this
